_comment: FRFRMU-1603 question-help companion — one entry per playbook/question-registry.json question_id (all 25), plus subject_type (asked at Rule 0, step-01-intake.md, before the registry's own field list starts). How this is used: playbook/asking-rules-help.md defines the ONE mechanism ('I don't know' and 'that's too thin' take the same path, chosen by shape); this file supplies the per-question tier/step/shape/example/idk_path that mechanism reads. Do NOT edit question-registry.json to add fields here — the FRFRMU-1309 pin compares only question_id + required_by_step. example_shape is written niche-neutral on purpose: asking-rules.md §2 rule 2 rewrites it in the creator's own niche at ask time (the re-render rule, asking-rules-help.md).

help.why_now: This decides whose business the whole plan is built around — get it wrong and every later answer is about the wrong brand.

example_shape.bad: leaving it implied instead of said out loud.
example_shape.good: one plain word: 'my own business' or 'a client I manage.'

help.idk_path: fact-propose — this is a plain yes/no-shaped gate, asked once at the very start, before any other question. There is no drafting path: only the creator knows the answer, so the agent simply asks plainly and waits.

help.why_now: This decides who every example, hook and word in your plan speaks to — get this wrong and the plan is for the wrong person.

example_shape.bad: a broad label with no situation, like 'business owners' or 'people who want to get better.'
example_shape.good: a situation plus a struggle, like 'a first-time manager who has never had to fire someone.'

help.idk_path: memory-look-first — the agent looks first at the account's own posts/comments and the website dossier for repeat descriptions of who shows up, drafts a candidate, and reads it back. Nothing found: ONE smaller, scene-shaped question ('picture your best client — one sentence about them'). Still nothing: deferred, with an instruction to note the next 5 people who reach out, and one line on what the plan loses meanwhile (a broader, less targeted draft).

help.why_now: Their audience's real words become your hooks — a vague problem makes vague, forgettable content.

example_shape.bad: a marketing-speak label, like 'they lack visibility' or 'they need more confidence.'
example_shape.good: the exact words a person would type in a DM at 11pm, like 'I keep starting and stopping and I don't know why.'

help.idk_path: memory-look-first — the agent looks at DMs, comments and reviews it already holds, drafts 2-3 candidate problems in the audience's own phrasing, and reads them back. Nothing found: one smaller question ('what's the last thing a customer complained about, in their own words?'). Still nothing: deferred, with an instruction to collect the next 10 DMs or comments before the next sitting.

help.why_now: This is the ONE thing that makes your content yours instead of a copy of everyone else's — it's what stops people scrolling past.

example_shape.bad: an adjective with nothing behind it, like 'quality service' or 'a different approach.'
example_shape.good: something tied to what you actually did or lived, naming your own method, for your one audience, that others in your space don't say.

help.idk_path: belief-draft (asking-rules.md §13) — draft from the creator's published sources and reviews, show 2-3 real examples from other businesses in their niche, give a plain-English process to work out their own, then read the draft back for a yes/no. Never saved unconfirmed.

help.why_now: A stance is what makes people remember you — a brand with no opinion is forgettable.

example_shape.bad: something nobody would argue with, like 'be consistent' or 'work hard.'
example_shape.good: something a chunk of people in your space would push back on, that you'd defend in a comment.

help.idk_path: belief-draft (asking-rules.md §13, the deepest 'unsure' case) — the same four-move protocol: draft from published sources, show 2-3 niche examples, give the plain-English process, read back for a yes/no. Includes the F3 pretend-counter-comment test once a stance is confirmed.

help.why_now: One real result is worth more than ten adjectives — it's the reason a stranger should believe you.

example_shape.bad: an adjective with no number, name or date, like 'I've helped a lot of people.'
example_shape.good: a number, a name, or a date, like 'one client went from 0 to 40,000 followers' or 'client X renewed for a third year.'

help.idk_path: memory-look-first, the worked example (founder, 2026-09-19). Never a dead end. The agent looks first — the creator's own posts, the website dossier, reviews found by WebSearch — and drafts a candidate. If genuinely nothing surfaces, it removes the pressure first ('it does not have to be impressive — one ordinary true thing beats a polished claim'), then asks smaller, concrete questions instead of repeating the ask: think of your oldest client — what were they like when they started, and what's different now? has anyone come back a second time, renewed, or sent a friend — who, and why? is there a message, review or screenshot from someone happy — what does it say? what's the smallest real change you've seen in someone, not the best one, the most ordinary one? Still nothing: deferred with a concrete collection instruction (e.g. 'next time someone says something good, screenshot it') and one plain line on what the plan loses meanwhile — it runs without a proof pillar until one is found.

help.why_now: This decides whether a 'comment KEYWORD' call-to-action is even allowed — asking for it without a working funnel sends people nowhere.

example_shape.bad: a bare yes/no with no detail, like 'yes we have that.'
example_shape.good: e.g. 'someone comments GUIDE under a reel and our tool sends them the link automatically — yes, and I tested it last week' or a plain 'no, we don't have that yet.'

help.idk_path: fact-propose — if it's unclear what's being asked, the agent explains it in one plain line first (e.g. 'someone comments a word under your post and a tool auto-sends them a link — do you have anything like that, tested?'), then proposes 'probably not yet' as a starting answer to confirm or correct, saved `derived` until confirmed.

help.why_now: Everything after this is built to hit ONE goal — chasing two at once usually gets neither.

example_shape.bad: no metric and no deadline, like 'grow.'
example_shape.good: a metric with a horizon, like '1,000 followers in 90 days to launch a course.'

help.idk_path: fact-propose — the agent proposes a goal from what it already holds (follower count, stage, any offer already mentioned) with its reason, e.g. 'I'd guess reach first, since the account is new — sound right?'. 'Don't know' makes the proposal the answer, saved `derived`, read back.

help.why_now: This sets the real, sustainable pace of the plan — a number bigger than you can keep up with just gets abandoned.

example_shape.bad: a motivated guess with no routine behind it, like 'daily, if I push myself.'
example_shape.good: a number tied to your actual week, like '2 a week — I film on Sundays.'

help.idk_path: fact-propose — the agent offers the fixed choices (2/week, 4/week, daily, other) with the honest note on each; 'don't know' defaults to proposing the lower, safer choice and reads it back for a confirm.

help.why_now: This sets the real starting point for what the plan can ask you to make — the market's favourite format still gets a path in, just not as the very first ask.

example_shape.bad: 'I can do anything' with no real detail.
example_shape.good: naming what you're actually comfortable with right now, like 'comfortable talking to camera, can't edit' — and if it's AI-generated, saying exactly what kind.

help.idk_path: fact-propose — the agent lists the concrete options (real people on camera, client footage, talking to camera, screen recording, graphics only, AI-generated), proposes the ones it can already see from the account, and reads them back for a yes/no or a correction.

help.why_now: Your niche and any seed accounts point Reach Machine at the right competitors to learn from — seeds are optional, and checked either way.

example_shape.bad: a category so broad it can't be searched, like 'food.'
example_shape.good: a phrase specific enough to search Instagram with, like 'meal prep for people who work night shifts' — seeds and hashtags are a bonus, not required.

help.idk_path: fact-propose — not knowing any seed accounts is a normal outcome: Step 2's own discovery finds accounts from the niche/hashtags without named seeds. Anything the creator DOES name is checked by the agent, never trusted blind.

help.why_now: Reach with nothing to point people at wastes the traffic — even a free next step is a real offer.

example_shape.bad: a vague label with no price or deliverable, like 'coaching.'
example_shape.good: an outcome, a timeframe and a price, like 'a 6-week program at a set price.'

help.idk_path: fact-propose — if the website already shows an offer, the agent leads with it and confirms. A reach-first creator with genuinely nothing may say so; the field stays empty and a later step (Step 7's advisory layer) fills it.

help.why_now: A plan that ignores what you can't say or show is a plan you can't actually use.

example_shape.bad: silence, or an unprompted 'no constraints' before the categories were even asked.
example_shape.good: a concrete list, or an explicit 'none of these apply' given AFTER hearing the categories.

help.idk_path: fact-propose, walked by category, one at a time (asking-rules.md §4/§14) — face on camera? claims you can't legally make? competitors you won't name? words or topics to avoid? each category gets its own small yes/no instead of one big blank question.

help.why_now: Your voice drives every hook and caption — 'professional and friendly' with nothing else describes everyone and no one.

example_shape.bad: two vague adjectives with nothing else, like 'authentic and professional.'
example_shape.good: 2-3 concrete descriptors plus a word to avoid or a reel you like, like 'direct, a little blunt, no corporate jargon — avoid the word "synergy".'

help.idk_path: belief-draft — the agent reads the account for tone (professional/casual/funny), drafts 2-3 descriptors from what it sees, and reads them back for a yes/no or a correction.

help.why_now: Content that builds toward something you already have coming (a launch, a promo, a season) works harder than content with nowhere to point.

example_shape.bad: 'maybe something later' with no date.
example_shape.good: a dated event, or an honest 'nothing in the next 8 weeks.'

help.idk_path: fact-propose — if nothing comes to mind, the agent MAY web-search the niche's seasonal/timely moments and propose 1-2 candidates to confirm.

help.why_now: So the plan doubles down on what already worked for you, and doesn't waste a slot re-trying what already flopped.

example_shape.bad: 'I've tried everything, nothing works.'
example_shape.good: one concrete win or flop with rough numbers, like 'a talking-head tip video died around 200 views, but one story-style post got 20,000.'

help.idk_path: memory-look-first — the agent looks at the account's own post history first and proposes what looks like a past win/flop from the numbers it can see, reads it back. Nothing found: ask for just one memory ('what's one post you were proud of, and one you wish you hadn't made?'). Still nothing: deferred, noting the plan starts with no track record to build on.

help.why_now: Your audience's own words, verbatim, become tomorrow's hooks — memory and paraphrase lose the exact phrasing that works.

example_shape.bad: a paraphrase from memory, like 'they ask about pricing.'
example_shape.good: 3-5 pasted, word-for-word questions or comments.

help.idk_path: memory-look-first — the agent checks comments/DMs it may already hold. Nothing found: ask for one remembered exact question. Still nothing: deferred, with an instruction to collect the last ~20 DMs or most-asked comments before the next sitting.

help.why_now: This is how many reels you'll actually write and check — the number is yours to pick, informed by a real recommendation.

example_shape.bad: the agent silently picking a number for you.
example_shape.good: a number YOU chose after hearing the trade-off, like 'twelve is fine — that's a longer session, not a bigger bill.'

help.idk_path: fact-propose — the agent proposes a number from your stage, cadence and horizon, states the honest trade-off (more writing and checking, never more credits), and reads it back for a yes/no.

help.why_now: Your real story is your highest-trust content — and it's optional, so nothing here is ever forced.

example_shape.bad: a summary with no scene, like 'I always loved helping people.'
example_shape.good: one specific, rememberable moment, like the exact day something changed.

help.idk_path: memory-look-first — the agent never invents a scene; it asks one question at a time from the reference ladder (backstory, the wall, the 5-Why drill, the point of no return), reacts to each answer before the next, and reads the assembled story back for a yes/no. Declining is always a complete, respected answer.

help.why_now: This is the language every caption and script in this plan gets written in — get it wrong and none of the words are usable.

example_shape.bad: a vague answer like 'whatever's easiest.'
example_shape.good: a named language, like 'English' or 'we post in Hindi.'

help.idk_path: fact-propose — if still vague after one more ask, the agent proposes the language the creator is talking in right now and records it as `derived`.

help.why_now: Your real follower count and posting history set the ceiling for what's realistic this month — guessing it wrong sets the wrong bar.

example_shape.bad: a vague label, like 'small account.'
example_shape.good: a real follower number plus posting history, like 'about 800 followers, posting on and off for 2 years.'

help.idk_path: fact-propose — once the account's own data has been pulled, the agent reads it and proposes the stage in one sentence for a yes/no, e.g. 'about 4,300 followers, posting roughly 3 times a week — sound right?'. Never asks for a number it already holds.

help.why_now: One clean sentence is the fastest way a stranger gets who you are — this just confirms the interview compressed to the right one.

example_shape.bad: a sentence a hundred other people could also say.
example_shape.good: a sentence with a specific scene in it that only you could say.

help.idk_path: memory-look-first — this compresses the personal-story interview already given. If it doesn't land, the agent proposes its own compression back for a yes or a one-word correction, never a new blank question.

help.why_now: The gap between where you were and where you are is what makes people trust you — polished-perfect is forgettable.

example_shape.bad: the agent proposing a flaw the creator never actually said.
example_shape.good: picking one from what you already told me, or saying 'none' — both are a complete answer.

help.idk_path: belief-draft, narrowed to what was already said — the agent only ever offers flaws the creator said in the interview, never invents one. 'None' is accepted at once and never revisited.

help.why_now: This tests whether your bold stance actually holds up when someone pushes back — words are easy, a real reply proves it.

example_shape.bad: backing down completely the moment someone disagrees.
example_shape.good: a one-sentence reply that holds the position, inside what you're comfortable saying publicly.

help.idk_path: belief-draft — the agent generates the likely counter-comment from the niche itself and asks for a real reply. A retreat softens the stance a notch to one you'll actually defend, never abandons it.

help.why_now: Small real moments are what make your content feel lived-in instead of generic — the lesson alone isn't a story.

example_shape.bad: a lesson with no moment behind it, like 'consistency matters.'
example_shape.good: a when/who/what in one line, like 'last week a client texted me at midnight, worried — I called back straight away, and that's the day they trusted me.'

help.idk_path: memory-look-first — the agent mines the personal-story interview for scenes already told. If none surface, it asks once more for the moment, not the lesson, and accepts fewer than five rather than inventing one.

help.why_now: Your voice needs a real test, not just a label — this checks a written line actually sounds like you.

example_shape.bad: agreeing a generic voice sounds right without really checking.
example_shape.good: naming the one word that's off, like 'that sounds too formal for me.'

help.idk_path: belief-draft — the agent writes one hook in the derived voice and asks whether it sounds right. Any 'off' word becomes a new item on the avoid list.
